java.at: Ride ride = new Ride(30, new PerMinuteRate());
java.say: Read this line from the inside out. `new PerMinuteRate()` makes a new object from the class PerMinuteRate. That object is the tariff: it knows how to price a ride by the minute.

Now `new Ride(...)` builds the ride, and Java runs the setup code of Ride. The ride stores its length, 30 minutes, and this line stores the tariff in the field `rate`. A field is a value that an object keeps. From now on, the ride holds on to its tariff.
The program asks the ride: what is your price? It does not say how to work it out, and it does not know which tariff the ride has.
Ride does not work out the price itself. It passes the question on to the tariff object it holds. `this` means "me": the ride sends itself along, so the tariff can look up how long the ride took.

The tariff's code runs now. Ride only knows its field as a RateStrategy, the interface. Java runs the code of the real object, a PerMinuteRate. With a DailyRate in the field, the DailyRate code would run here instead.
To work out the price, the tariff needs the length of the ride, so it asks the ride. The ride answers: 30 minutes.
Back in the tariff: 30 × 0.25 = 7.50. `return` hands the answer back to whoever asked, here the ride.
The ride hands 7.50 back to the program. Ride holds no price rule at all; it only knows whom to ask.
The program prints the price (Java writes 7.50 as 7.5). A weekend tariff is one new class. Ride and this program stay as they are.
